slides.headline: ORIG_HEAD
slides.body: In one sentence: a file that holds the commit HEAD, your current position, pointed at before the last "drastic" command, so that the command can be undone with git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD.

slides.headline: ORIG_HEAD
slides.body: git pull writes it too, because it runs a merge or a rebase, and so does git stash push, through the reset it performs.

slides.headline: git fsck as a search tool
slides.body: In one sentence: git fsck walks the object database from every starting point and reports what it can't reach.

slides.headline: git fsck as a search tool
slides.body: Four options matter. The default, --dangling, reports unreachable objects that no other object refers to: the tips of lost history, and blobs that lost their index entry.

slides.direction: The first root-cause box of section 13.4.
slides.text:
Observed behavior : "git reflog show main" starts at "Add embedding client", but main points at dfcbd4b
Git state         : refs/heads/main = dfcbd4b; the newest line left in logs/refs/heads/main records 536f5df
Mechanism         : reflog expiry removed every entry with an end that the current tip does not reach,
                    including the entries that moved the branch to its current value
Root cause        : a reflog is a list of past changes that is trimmed by a retention policy; it is not
                    a second copy of the ref
Why Git does this : such changes "are not part of the current project", so "most users will want to
                    expire them sooner" (git help gc)
Correct fix       : none needed; the ref is right and the log is shorter
Prevention        : anchor anything you may want later with a branch or tag before the 30 days are over

slides.direction: The second root-cause box of section 13.4.
slides.text:
Observed behavior : "git stash list" prints nothing after "git reflog expire --expire=now --all"
Git state         : refs/stash still points at 71ed40a, the newest entry; its log is empty;
                    the older entry 89fc6b8 is a dangling commit
Mechanism         : "git stash list" prints the reflog of refs/stash. The command emptied the log
                    and left the ref alone
Root cause        : only the newest stash entry is held by a ref. Every older entry is held by a
                    reflog line and by nothing else
Why Git does this : the stash was built as one ref plus its reflog, so that "stash@{n}" is ordinary
                    reflog syntax
Correct fix       : "git stash pop" still restores the newest entry (below). The older ones are found
                    with git fsck while their objects exist
Prevention        : do not expire reflogs with --all in a repository that holds stashes you need;
                    commit long-lived work to a branch instead of stashing it

slides.direction: 🔴 DANGEROUS: `git branch -D`. The five answers, from the command safety table of the chapter. What it changes: it deletes a ref together with that ref's reflog. What it can destroy: the only name of commits that were never merged; it deletes no object. How to preview: use `git branch -d`, which refuses when the branch is not fully merged. How to recover: recreate the ref at the old tip, while the objects exist; that is the next video. When it is appropriate: when you have read the refusal of `-d` and decided the commits are not needed.

slides.body: Five mistakes to watch for.

items: "30 days in the reflog, then two more weeks." Root cause: the prune cut-off is compared with the modification time of the object file, not with the moment the object became unreachable.
Expecting a deleted branch's reflog to still exist. Root cause: git branch -d and -D delete the reflog with the branch; only the HEAD reflog, or git fsck, still knows the tip.
git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD some commands later. Root cause: ORIG_HEAD is one slot written by a short list of commands, and it keeps the value of an earlier one after commands that do not write it.

"git fsck shows nothing, so the commits are gone." Root cause: by default reflog entries count as starting points, so commits that a reflog still names are not reported; --no-reflogs removes them from the roots.
Reading "dangling" as damage. Root cause: dangling is information; only lines that begin with missing, broken or error describe a repository that needs repair.

slides.label: Q192
quotes: State the default retention periods, say which event starts each period, and explain why "30 days plus two weeks" is not a guarantee.

slides.lead: Let's land this. You should now be able to say:
items: By default reflog entries last 90 days, 30 days if an end is off the current history, and unreachable objects older than two weeks can be pruned; none of it happens until a command runs.
A deleted branch, a bare repository, a tag and a branch that was only fetched have no reflog to recover from.
ORIG_HEAD is one slot written by reset, merge, rebase and am; I use it only as the very next command, and the branch reflog otherwise.
git fsck --no-reflogs lists what no ref reaches; a dangling commit is the tip of a lost chain.
A found commit is safe only after I give it a ref.

beats.text: That was the CTO's second question in the last video, about work lost in a Git repository. The common answer in engineering chat is "relax, Git keeps everything for 30 days, plus two weeks". Three things are wrong with that sentence.
beats.tele: That was the CTO's second question in the last video, about work lost in a Git repository. The common answer in engineering chat is "relax, Git keeps everything for 30 days, plus two weeks". Three things are wrong with that sentence.

beats.text: Nothing happens when the time is up. Expiry is work done by a command. The two weeks aren't added on top of the 30 days. And there are situations in which there was never a reflog entry to begin with: a deleted branch, a server, a tag, a branch you only fetched. The reflog, remember, is Git's local log of where each name has pointed.
beats.tele: Nothing happens when the time is up. Expiry is work done by a command. The two weeks aren't added on top of the 30 days. And there are situations in which there was never a reflog entry to begin with: a deleted branch, a server, a tag, a branch you only fetched. The reflog, remember, is Git's local log of where each name has pointed.

beats.text: If you give the CTO the comfortable number and the work was in one of those situations, you'll be wrong at the moment it matters. Keep that comfortable sentence in mind. By the end you can correct it.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. Last time you learned the four layers that protect a commit, a saved snapshot of your project: refs, reflogs, a grace period, and other repositories. And you learned how to read a reflog.
beats.tele: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. Last time you learned the four layers that protect a commit, a saved snapshot of your project: refs, reflogs, a grace period, and other repositories. And you learned how to read a reflog.

beats.text: Today you learn how long layers two and three last, and what shortens them. Then two instruments. ORIG_HEAD, which is convenient and holds exactly one value. And git fsck, which you met as an integrity check and now use as a search tool for work that no ref and no reflog names.
beats.tele: Today you learn how long layers two and three last, and what shortens them. Then two instruments. `ORIG_HEAD`, which is convenient and holds exactly one value. And `git fsck`, which you met as an integrity check and now use as a search tool for work that no ref and no reflog names.

beats.text: One remark about the demonstrations, said once. The lab clock is fixed in the past and the expiry code reads the real clock, so the lab configuration sets the two reflog periods to never. The 90 and 30 days are stated from the manual. On screen, expiry is shown only with the cut-off now, which doesn't depend on a clock. A relative cut-off would depend on the recording date.
beats.tele: One remark about the demonstrations, said once. The lab clock is fixed in the past and the expiry code reads the real clock, so the lab configuration sets the two reflog periods to `never`. The 90 and 30 days are stated from the manual. On screen, expiry is shown only with the cut-off `now`, which doesn't depend on a clock. A relative cut-off would depend on the recording date.

beats.tele: state the default retention periods and which event starts each;

beats.tele: name the situations in which no reflog exists or it is deleted at once;

beats.text: say which four commands write ORIG_HEAD and why it is one slot;
beats.tele: say which four commands write `ORIG_HEAD` and why it is one slot;

beats.text: find lost commits with git fsck and explain --no-reflogs;
beats.tele: find lost commits with `git fsck` and explain `--no-reflogs`;

beats.text: The defaults. Three numbers govern recoverability in a repository with default configuration.
beats.tele: The defaults. Three numbers govern recoverability in a repository with default configuration.

beats.text: Two facts about these numbers are routinely misunderstood.
beats.tele: Two facts about these numbers are routinely misunderstood.

beats.text: First, nothing happens when the time is up. Expiry is work done by a command: git gc, Git's garbage collection, git reflog expire, or the maintenance that Git starts after some commands. An entry that is 100 days old is still there until one of them runs.
beats.tele: First, nothing happens when the time is up. Expiry is work done by a command: `git gc`, Git's garbage collection, `git reflog expire`, or the maintenance that Git starts after some commands. An entry that is 100 days old is still there until one of them runs.

beats.text: Second, the 30-day rule is the one that matters for recovery, because it applies to the entries you recover from. The manual says such entries "are generally created as a result of using git commit --amend or git rebase and are the commits prior to the amend or rebase occurring". The exact test, from the source: an entry is subject to the shorter period if its old value or its new value isn't reachable from the ref's current tip.
beats.tele: Second, the 30-day rule is the one that matters for recovery, because it applies to the entries you recover from. The manual says such entries "are generally created as a result of using `git commit --amend` or `git rebase` and are the commits prior to the amend or rebase occurring". The exact test, from the source: an entry is subject to the shorter period if its old value or its new value isn't reachable from the ref's current tip.

beats.text: The grace period isn't added on top. gc.pruneExpire compares the cut-off with the modification time of the object file. The two weeks are measured against that modification time, not from the moment the object became unreachable.
beats.tele: The grace period isn't added on top. `gc.pruneExpire` compares the cut-off with the modification time of the object file. The two weeks are measured against that modification time, not from the moment the object became unreachable.

beats.text: Try it now, on paper. Thirty seconds: a commit was written 40 days ago and hasn't been touched since. Today it loses its last reflog entry. How much grace period is left? Say it out loud.
beats.tele: Try it now, on paper. Thirty seconds: a commit was written 40 days ago and hasn't been touched since. Today it loses its last reflog entry. How much grace period is left? Say it out loud.

beats.text: Possibly none. That commit may already be older than the cut-off. The grace period protects what never had a reflog entry and was written recently.
beats.tele: Possibly none. That commit may already be older than the cut-off. The grace period protects what never had a reflog entry and was written recently.

beats.text: The exceptions. Four situations give you less than the table promises, and one gives you more.
beats.tele: The exceptions. Four situations give you less than the table promises, and one gives you more.

beats.text: A deleted branch loses its reflog at once. The manual of git branch says so for -d and -D. The commits stay reachable from the HEAD reflog if you ever had the branch checked out. The same holds for a remote-tracking branch that git fetch --prune removes.
beats.tele: A deleted branch loses its reflog at once. The manual of `git branch` says so for `-d` and `-D`. The commits stay reachable from the HEAD reflog if you ever had the branch checked out. The same holds for a remote-tracking branch that `git fetch --prune` removes.

beats.text: A commit that was never checked out has no HEAD reflog entry. A teammate's branch that you only fetched exists in your clone as a remote-tracking ref. When that ref is pruned, nothing names the commits, and they are on layer three from that moment.
beats.tele: A commit that was never checked out has no HEAD reflog entry. A teammate's branch that you only fetched exists in your clone as a remote-tracking ref. When that ref is pruned, nothing names the commits, and they are on layer three from that moment.

beats.text: A bare repository, one with no working tree, as on a server, keeps no reflogs by default. core.logAllRefUpdates is true by default in a repository with a working tree and false by default in a bare repository. A server that receives a force push therefore has no record of the value that was overwritten.
beats.tele: A bare repository, one with no working tree, as on a server, keeps no reflogs by default. `core.logAllRefUpdates` is true by default in a repository with a working tree and false by default in a bare repository. A server that receives a force push therefore has no record of the value that was overwritten.

beats.text: Tags, the fixed names for commits, have no reflog. Moving a tag with git tag -f prints the old ID once, and that line is the only record.
beats.tele: Tags, the fixed names for commits, have no reflog. Moving a tag with `git tag -f` prints the old ID once, and that line is the only record.

beats.text: And the one that gives you more: stash entries, your parked uncommitted work, don't expire, until they are dropped. The textbook cites a comment in Git's source for this, "If unconfigured, make stash never expire", and notes that no manual page states it. The exemption applies to the default periods only. A cut-off given on the command line applies to every ref, refs/stash included.
beats.tele: And the one that gives you more: stash entries, your parked uncommitted work, don't expire, until they are dropped. The textbook cites a comment in Git's source for this, "If unconfigured, make stash never expire", and notes that no manual page states it. The exemption applies to the default periods only. A cut-off given on the command line applies to every ref, `refs/stash` included.

beats.text: ORIG_HEAD. In one sentence: a file that holds the commit HEAD, your current position, pointed at before the last "drastic" command, so that the command can be undone with git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD. The manual names four commands: git am, git merge, git rebase, git reset.
beats.tele: `ORIG_HEAD`. In one sentence: a file that holds the commit HEAD, your current position, pointed at before the last "drastic" command, so that the command can be undone with `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD`. The manual names four commands: `git am`, `git merge`, `git rebase`, `git reset`.

beats.text: git pull writes it too, because it runs a merge or a rebase, and so does git stash push, through the reset it performs. Inside .git it's one file with one ID. It has no reflog, and it's not a starting point for garbage collection.
beats.tele: `git pull` writes it too, because it runs a merge or a rebase, and so does `git stash push`, through the reset it performs. Inside `.git` it's one file with one ID. It has no reflog, and it's not a starting point for garbage collection.

beats.text: git fsck as a search tool. In one sentence: git fsck walks the object database from every starting point and reports what it can't reach. 🟢 SAFE, except that --lost-found writes files into .git/lost-found.
beats.tele: `git fsck` as a search tool. In one sentence: `git fsck` walks the object database from every starting point and reports what it can't reach. 🟢 SAFE, except that `--lost-found` writes files into `.git/lost-found`.

beats.text: Four options matter. The default, --dangling, reports unreachable objects that no other object refers to: the tips of lost history, and blobs that lost their index entry. --unreachable reports every unreachable object. --no-reflogs doesn't count reflog entries as starting points. And --lost-found also writes each dangling commit's ID and each dangling blob's content into files.
beats.tele: Four options matter. The default, `--dangling`, reports unreachable objects that no other object refers to: the tips of lost history, and blobs that lost their index entry. `--unreachable` reports every unreachable object. `--no-reflogs` doesn't count reflog entries as starting points. And `--lost-found` also writes each dangling commit's ID and each dangling blob's content into files.

beats.text: The difference between "dangling" and "unreachable" is the difference between a tip and a chain. On screen, the three commits of the branch exp/hybrid from today's demonstration, after its deletion. If three commits are lost, all three are unreachable, and only the newest is dangling, because the newest still refers to the other two. For recovery you want dangling commits: anchor the tip and the chain comes with it.
beats.tele: The difference between "dangling" and "unreachable" is the difference between a tip and a chain. On screen, the three commits of the branch `exp/hybrid` from today's demonstration, after its deletion. If three commits are lost, all three are unreachable, and only the newest is dangling, because the newest still refers to the other two. For recovery you want dangling commits: anchor the tip and the chain comes with it.

beats.text: Now a picture to keep. For ORIG_HEAD the textbook's analogy is the "last number redial" button of a phone. It holds exactly one number, the newest call replaces it, and it tells you nothing about which call that was. The reflog is the full call list.
beats.tele: Now a picture to keep. For `ORIG_HEAD` the textbook's analogy is the "last number redial" button of a phone. It holds exactly one number, the newest call replaces it, and it tells you nothing about which call that was. The reflog is the full call list.

beats.text: Carry the vault from the last video for the rest. A reflog is a ledger that is trimmed by a retention policy. It's not a second copy of the ref. And git fsck is the audit that walks the vault with every card and every ledger line in hand and lists the boxes nobody mentions. With --no-reflogs, the auditor leaves the ledger at the desk and uses the cards only.
beats.tele: Carry the vault from the last video for the rest. A reflog is a ledger that is trimmed by a retention policy. It's not a second copy of the ref. And `git fsck` is the audit that walks the vault with every card and every ledger line in hand and lists the boxes nobody mentions. With `--no-reflogs`, the auditor leaves the ledger at the desk and uses the cards only.

beats.text: Where the redial button breaks as a model: a phone's last number is at least always the last call. ORIG_HEAD is the position before the last command from a short list. After a commit, a switch or a cherry-pick it still holds a value from some earlier command.
beats.tele: Where the redial button breaks as a model: a phone's last number is at least always the last call. `ORIG_HEAD` is the position before the last command from a short list. After a commit, a switch or a cherry-pick it still holds a value from some earlier command.

beats.text: Stop on the third row. After day 30 the next maintenance run removes the reflog entries, and because the object file is already older than two weeks, the same run may delete the object. There's no second waiting period.
beats.tele: Stop on the third row. After day 30 the next maintenance run removes the reflog entries, and because the object file is already older than two weeks, the same run may delete the object. There's no second waiting period.

beats.text: Three commits in a chain. All three are unreachable. Only 2ae0c97 is dangling. The blob on the right is both: it was staged, and then its index entry was reset.
beats.tele: Three commits in a chain. All three are unreachable. Only `2ae0c97` is dangling. The blob on the right is both: it was staged, and then its index entry was reset.

beats.text: Here's that branch as a picture: three commits, an amend, one more commit, and a reset. Two commits end up off the current history.
beats.tele: Here's that branch as a picture: three commits, an amend, one more commit, and a reset. Two commits end up off the current history.

beats.text: Predict: of six entries, how many fall under the 30-day rule? Say it out loud. I'll wait.
beats.tele: Predict: of six entries, how many fall under the 30-day rule? Say it out loud. I'll wait.

beats.text: Four of six. The commit before the amend, the commit that was reset away, and also the two entries whose other end is one of those commits. Despite the word prune in the output, the dry run removed nothing.
beats.tele: Four of six. The commit before the amend, the commit that was reset away, and also the two entries whose other end is one of those commits. Despite the word `prune` in the output, the dry run removed nothing.

beats.text: The HEAD reflog wasn't named in that command and still has every entry. In a real repository both logs are trimmed in the same run.
beats.tele: The HEAD reflog wasn't named in that command and still has every entry. In a real repository both logs are trimmed in the same run.

beats.text: Now the stash. Two entries.
beats.tele: Now the stash. Two entries.

beats.text: The stash list is the reflog of refs/stash. Predict what git stash list prints after a cut-off of now is applied to all refs.
beats.tele: The stash list is the reflog of `refs/stash`. Predict what `git stash list` prints after a cut-off of `now` is applied to all refs.

beats.text: Nothing. The ref still points at 71ed40a, the newest entry. The older entry, 89fc6b8, is now a dangling commit.
beats.tele: Nothing. The ref still points at `71ed40a`, the newest entry. The older entry, `89fc6b8`, is now a dangling commit.

beats.text: And the two commits from the picture are in that list as well.
beats.tele: And the two commits from the picture are in that list as well.

beats.text: The newest entry comes back. You recover an older one in the video on uncommitted work.
beats.tele: The newest entry comes back. You recover an older one in the video on uncommitted work.

beats.text: The server. A push into a bare repository.
beats.tele: The server. A push into a bare repository.

beats.text: No reflogs on the bare side. The setting isn't set there. Whoever administers a bare repository can switch it on. git config set and git config get need Git 2.46 or later.
beats.tele: No reflogs on the bare side. The setting isn't set there. Whoever administers a bare repository can switch it on. `git config set` and `git config get` need Git 2.46 or later.

beats.text: The log has one line, and main@{1} still resolves: Git takes the old value recorded in that line. This is a setting for servers you run yourself. A hosting service has its own instruments, which come at the end of this module.
beats.tele: The log has one line, and `main@{1}` still resolves: Git takes the old value recorded in that line. This is a setting for servers you run yourself. A hosting service has its own instruments, which come at the end of this module.

beats.text: An amend, two switches, a cherry-pick and a revert: five movements of HEAD, each with a reflog entry, and no ORIG_HEAD. A reset, a merge and a rebase each write it.
beats.tele: An amend, two switches, a cherry-pick and a revert: five movements of HEAD, each with a reflog entry, and no `ORIG_HEAD`. A reset, a merge and a rebase each write it.

beats.text: Each time the value is the tip from immediately before the command. Now the trap. You switch to main and cherry-pick. Quick quiz, three options. Does ORIG_HEAD name the tip of main before the cherry-pick, the old tip of the feature branch, or nothing? Say it out loud.
beats.tele: Each time the value is the tip from immediately before the command. Now the trap. You switch to `main` and cherry-pick. Quick quiz, three options. Does `ORIG_HEAD` name the tip of `main` before the cherry-pick, the old tip of the feature branch, or nothing? Say it out loud.

beats.text: Option two. 68e6fff, a commit of the feature branch from before its rebase, which no branch contains any more.
beats.tele: Option two. `68e6fff`, a commit of the feature branch from before its rebase, which no branch contains any more.

beats.text: git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD at this moment would move main onto abandoned history. On the picture, ORIG_HEAD sits on a dashed commit that no branch contains. Almost everyone trusts it once too often.
beats.tele: `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` at this moment would move `main` onto abandoned history. On the picture, `ORIG_HEAD` sits on a dashed commit that no branch contains. Almost everyone trusts it once too often.

beats.text: Predict: does git fsck report the three commits? Say it out loud.
beats.tele: Predict: does `git fsck` report the three commits? Say it out loud.

beats.text: No. Only the blob, the content of one file. The three commits are still reachable from the HEAD reflog, because the branch was checked out when they were made. That default answers "what is at risk of being collected?". To ask "what is no longer on any branch?", take the reflogs out.
beats.tele: No. Only the blob, the content of one file. The three commits are still reachable from the HEAD reflog, because the branch was checked out when they were made. That default answers "what is at risk of being collected?". To ask "what is no longer on any branch?", take the reflogs out.

beats.text: One dangling commit, 2ae0c97, stands for three unreachable commits with their trees and blobs.
beats.tele: One dangling commit, `2ae0c97`, stands for three unreachable commits with their trees and blobs.

beats.text: In a repository that has been used for months the list of dangling commits is long: every amend, every rebase and every dropped stash leaves one. Turn the list into something you can read.
beats.tele: In a repository that has been used for months the list of dangling commits is long: every amend, every rebase and every dropped stash leaves one. Turn the list into something you can read.

beats.text: Date, author, subject for each tip. The second command shows the whole lost line: commits reachable from the found tip and from no ref.
beats.tele: Date, author, subject for each tip. The second command shows the whole lost line: commits reachable from the found tip and from no ref.

beats.text: --lost-found saves the findings as files. That's convenient for blobs: a blob has no name and no date and can only be recognised by its content.
beats.tele: `--lost-found` saves the findings as files. That's convenient for blobs: a blob has no name and no date and can only be recognised by its content.

beats.text: A found commit is still unreachable. Reading it doesn't protect it. Give it a ref. 🟢 SAFE: git branch <name> <id> writes one ref and changes nothing else.
beats.tele: A found commit is still unreachable. Reading it doesn't protect it. Give it a ref. 🟢 SAFE: `git branch <name> <id>` writes one ref and changes nothing else.

beats.text: From this moment the three commits are on layer one, and no expiry or collection can touch them. One label on the tip, and the whole chain is solid again.
beats.tele: From this moment the three commits are on layer one, and no expiry or collection can touch them. One label on the tip, and the whole chain is solid again.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: "30 days in the reflog, then two more weeks." Root cause: the prune cut-off is compared with the modification time of the object file, not with the moment the object became unreachable.
beats.tele: "30 days in the reflog, then two more weeks." Root cause: the prune cut-off is compared with the modification time of the object file, not with the moment the object became unreachable.

beats.text: Expecting a deleted branch's reflog to still exist. Root cause: git branch -d and -D delete the reflog with the branch; only the HEAD reflog, or git fsck, still knows the tip.
beats.tele: Expecting a deleted branch's reflog to still exist. Root cause: `git branch -d` and `-D` delete the reflog with the branch; only the HEAD reflog, or `git fsck`, still knows the tip.

beats.text: git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD some commands later. Root cause: ORIG_HEAD is one slot written by a short list of commands, and it keeps the value of an earlier one after commands that do not write it.
beats.tele: `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` some commands later. Root cause: `ORIG_HEAD` is one slot written by a short list of commands, and it keeps the value of an earlier one after commands that do not write it.

beats.text: "git fsck shows nothing, so the commits are gone." Root cause: by default reflog entries count as starting points, so commits that a reflog still names are not reported; --no-reflogs removes them from the roots.
beats.tele: "`git fsck` shows nothing, so the commits are gone." Root cause: by default reflog entries count as starting points, so commits that a reflog still names are not reported; `--no-reflogs` removes them from the roots.

beats.text: Reading "dangling" as damage. Root cause: dangling is information; only lines that begin with missing, broken or error describe a repository that needs repair.

beats.text: The lead reads the state before anyone types more. refs/stash still points at the newest entry, so one experiment comes back with git stash pop. The other three were held by reflog lines only. They're dangling commits now, on layer three, and nothing has been pruned yet. The team finds them with git fsck, anchors each one, and writes down the rule that the root-cause box gives: long-lived work goes on a branch, not into the stash, and nobody expires reflogs with --all in a repository that holds work.
